The correct fix — explicitly removing frozen parameters from the optimizer's parameter groups before ZeRO state initialization, as recommended in the HuggingFace PEFT + DeepSpeed integration guides — avoids the problem entirely, but retrofitting this after training has started requires tearing down and reinitializing the ZeRO optimizer, which most training loops do not support gracefully.

DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 builds its all-gather schedule at initialization by walking the model's named_parameters() in registration order and assigning each parameter a ds_id — a global flat index that determines which rank owns that parameter's shard and when its all-gather must fire relative to forward pass layer execution. When you remove frozen parameters from optimizer groups but still need their values during the forward pass, the ds_id sequence develops gaps: the remaining trainable parameters get contiguous shard assignments, but the frozen parameters — which DeepSpeed still needs to all-gather for forward computation — are registered separately as external_param or handled via the GatheredParameters context manager, breaking the assumption that shard boundaries align cleanly with layer execution order. The practical consequence is that the prefetch engine, which looks ahead one or two layers and pre-issues all-gathers to overlap communication with compute, now operates on a split registry: it must track trainable-parameter shards through the normal ZeRO partition schedule and frozen-parameter tensors through a separate pathway, and any misalignment in the prefetch cursor means a layer stalls waiting for an all-gather that was supposed to have already completed. DeepSpeed resolves this in the zero.Init context by tagging frozen parameters with ds_persist=True or keeping them in a non-partitioned "persistent parameter" pool that is broadcast once at initialization and held in full on every rank, sidestepping the all-gather schedule entirely at the cost of replicating those tensors across all ranks — effectively reverting those parameters to ZeRO-1 semantics. This design is documented in the DeepSpeed ZeRO-Infinity paper (Rajbhandari et al., 2021) as the "persistent parameter" mechanism, and it means that a model with 80% frozen layers under this scheme pays the full memory cost of those frozen weights on every rank, which can negate much of ZeRO-3's memory savings if the frozen portion is large. The tension is fundamental: ZeRO-3's communication schedule is designed around the invariant that every parameter is sharded and gathered on demand, and frozen parameters that live outside the optimizer violate that invariant, forcing a choice between schedule complexity (non-contiguous ds_id gaps with split prefetch tracking) and memory redundancy (persistent full replication).

Large embedding tables in transformer LLMs are weight-tied or input-only, meaning their forward pass produces an activation tensor of shape [batch, seq_len, vocab_size] at the logit projection layer — for a vocabulary of 128K tokens (LLaMA-3 scale) with batch 4 and sequence 4096, that single logit tensor is 4 × 4096 × 128000 × 2 bytes ≈ 4.2 GB per rank, and this is additive with the replicated embedding weight itself (128000 × 8192 × 2 bytes ≈ 2.1 GB for a 8192-dim model). When those embedding weights are marked ds_persist=True, every rank holds the full 2.1 GB weight redundantly, but more damagingly, the logit activation cannot be sharded during the forward pass without a subsequent all-reduce — so peak activation memory spikes by the full logit tensor size simultaneously with the persistent weight sitting in memory, and these two allocations coexist at the same point in the forward pass. The crossover point where this exceeds ZeRO-3's gradient savings is straightforward to estimate: ZeRO-3 across N ranks saves (N-1)/N of gradient memory for trainable parameters, so on 64 ranks each rank holds 1/64 of gradients — for a 7B trainable parameter model in FP16 that's roughly 7B × 2 / 64 ≈ 219 MB of gradient memory per rank saved versus baseline. The 4.2 GB logit activation spike dwarfs that saving by nearly 20×, meaning the activation pressure from a replicated frozen embedding table operating at reasonable batch sizes eliminates any memory headroom ZeRO-3 created for the trainable adapter layers. This is precisely the failure mode observed in practice when fine-tuning models like BLOOM-176B with frozen embeddings under DeepSpeed ZeRO-3: the embedding and unembedding tables together account for over 7 GB at bf16, and with logit activations the peak memory per rank during the final linear layer exceeds what would be needed if those parameters had simply been left in the ZeRO-3 shard schedule and gathered on demand. The correct mitigation is vocab parallelism (tensor-parallel column sharding of the embedding table across ranks, as in Megatron-LM's VocabParallelEmbedding) combined with sequence-parallel logit computation, which keeps both the weight and the activation sharded — but this requires tight integration between the tensor-parallel and ZeRO-3 communication schedules that DeepSpeed's ds_persist pathway was explicitly designed to avoid.
